title: Catégorie des types de mots [dont arbres plans] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This is the first page of the dossier. It is a sketch sheet: mostly drawings, with a few captioned boxes. Read together with p.2, the project is a combinatorial-topological model for 'types of words' in a free group (letters u, v, ... and inverses).

(1) Top strip. A horizontal path s_0 -> s_1 -> s_2 -> s_3 -> s_4 has bouquets of petals labelled W attached at each vertex, and further W's on the edges. This is the standard normal form of an arbitrary word: a freely reduced 'spine' (the s_i) with subwords W that freely reduce to 1 inserted at each position. The arrows u^{-1}W <-> uW at the double-headed arrow mid-page express the same 'insert a trivial word' freedom.

(2) Boxed catalogue. Each word type is drawn as a circle with an origin arrow and marked points on the boundary, one per letter.
- Empty circle: 'identité', the empty word; count 1.
- One point: 'lettre u ou lettre inverse u^{-1}'; count 2.
- Two points: the four length-2 words uu, u^{-1}u, uu^{-1}, u^{-1}u^{-1}.
- Three points: 'système de trois lettres'.
- A circle with a chord joining the two points: 'syst. u^{-1}u ou uu^{-1}'; count 2. The chord records a cancelling pair.

So a type of word is a disc with n marked boundary points (the letters) and a family of disjoint, i.e. non-crossing, chords. The chords record which letters cancel against which in free reduction. Page 2 states this as an equivalence:
- the category of word types of length n is equivalent to the isotopy category of triples (D, ω, K) plus a marked set S of boundary points;
- D is an oriented disc and K is a chord decomposition, with conditions on how many points of S lie on each boundary arc;
- 'ordre réduit' = Σ_α (card(α∩S) − 1);
- 'trivial' means reduced order 0; 'reduced' means K = ∅.

(3) Dual picture: trees. Non-crossing chord dissections of a disc are dual to plane trees inscribed in it ('arbres circonscrits'). A word that reduces to 1 traces a closed walk in the Cayley tree of the free group; its image is a plane tree, and the word is the contour walk of that tree. The left-hand drawings show trees with arrows running along both sides of the edges, i.e. contour walks.

The big circles with trees hanging off them (top left, right side, bottom middle) depict cyclic words. Each is a cyclically reduced core (the circle, with 'sommets principaux' marked) plus hanging trees: the cancelling parts.

(4) Operations boxes. These read 'composition avec ⟲ / inversion de ⟲(chord)' and 'composition / inversion d'un cycle', with marginal labels that probably say 'op. id.' and 'op. inv.' They indicate the groupoid-like operations on types: concatenation and formal inverse (reversing orientation and swapping u <-> u^{-1}).

(5) Bottom. '(Γ_i)_{i∈I} famille d'arbres plans; Γ_i, Γ_j; s_ij sommet de Γ_i'. This sets up gluing a family of plane trees at specified vertices (grafting). It is the operadic or 'tree of trees' composition needed to build the category's morphisms or to describe nested cancellation.

Purpose: to give an intrinsic, isotopy-invariant description of combinatorial word types (free-reduction patterns) via discs with chord dissections and dual plane trees. This fits Grothendieck's 1981–84 interest in plane trees, maps and dessins.
errors: No mathematical errors are visible; the page is sketches without claims.
The precise definition of morphisms in the 'catégorie des types de mots' is not stated on this page, so the category structure cannot be checked here.
The admissibility conditions (each boundary arc carries at least one, or at most one, marked point) are only fixed on p.2, where Grothendieck himself hesitates ('au choix').

ideas.what: Encoding the cancellation pattern of a word in a free group by non-crossing chords on a disc with marked boundary points (one per letter)
ideas.modern_name: Non-crossing matchings/partitions as free-reduction patterns (used e.g. in free probability for Haar unitaries/free group moments, and in counting trivial words)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical combinatorics (Kreweras 1972 for non-crossing partitions); free-probability use by Voiculescu, Speicher, Nica (1980s–90s)

ideas.what: Words reducing to 1 as contour walks of plane trees (closed walks in the Cayley tree); duality between chord dissections of a disc and plane trees
ideas.modern_name: Contour walk / Dyck path bijection; dual tree of a polygon dissection
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Catalan combinatorics; Harary–Tutte era; Stasheff for dissections and trees)
ideas.where_published: Plane trees appear in Esquisse d'un programme (1984) in the context of dessins/Shabat polynomials, but not this word-theoretic use

ideas.what: A word as a reduced spine s_0…s_k with trivial subwords W inserted at each vertex; a cyclic word as a cyclically reduced core cycle with hanging trees
ideas.modern_name: Free reduction normal form; core graph plus hanging trees (Stallings folding picture)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical free group theory; graph-theoretic formulation by Stallings ('Topology of finite graphs', 1983)

ideas.what: A category of word types equivalent to an isotopy category of oriented discs with chord decompositions and marked boundary points; 'ordre réduit' as an invariant
ideas.modern_name: Combinatorial maps / chord diagram categories; close to categories of planar (non-crossing) partitions
ideas.usually_credited_to: No single attribution; related structures appear in planar algebras (Jones, 1999) and in categories of non-crossing partitions (Banica–Speicher, 2009)

ideas.what: Grafting a family of plane trees (Γ_i) at specified vertices s_ij

missed.claim: Around 1982 Grothendieck links free-group word combinatorics (free reduction, cyclic reduction to a core with hanging trees) to the topological data of discs with chord dissections and plane trees, his 'arbres plans'. This is the same circle of ideas as Stallings' folding (1983) and as the non-crossing partition combinatorics later central to free probability. These notes connect it explicitly to the plane-tree/dessin programme. The link between dessins (plane trees, Shabat polynomials) and free-reduction patterns or non-crossing partitions does not seem to be made in the literature from Grothendieck's side.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is mostly of historical interest. It documents that Grothendieck's plane-tree combinatorics grew partly out of word combinatorics in free groups, which is relevant to the π_1 of P^1 minus three points and the Galois-action-on-trees viewpoint. Its mathematical content is classical.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a minor thread. Comparable categorical structures (categories of non-crossing partitions, planar algebras) were developed independently later.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a sketch page of classical combinatorics: free reduction, non-crossing chords, contour walks of plane trees. It is historically interesting as the opening of a dossier tying word types to plane trees around 1982, contemporaneous with Stallings' graph methods and preceding free-probability combinatorics. But there is no result here that a specialist would find new.
transcription_corrections: The numbers '1' and '2' beside the boxes are counts of word types: 1 for the identity, 2 for 'u or u^{-1}', 2 for 'u^{-1}u or uu^{-1}'. They are not section labels.
'u^{-1}W uτW[?]' near the double-headed arrow is more likely 'u^{-1}W uW' (or 'u^{-1}w … uw'), labelling the two directions of the arrow.
The marginal labels 'opp.[?] idé[?]' and 'opp.[?] init.[?]' are probably 'op. id.' and 'op. inv.' (operation identity / operation inverse), matching the boxes 'composition avec ⟲' and 'inversion …'.
'système de deux lettres' rather than 'dans lettres'; the four listed words are uu, u^{-1}u, uu^{-1}, u^{-1}u^{-1}.
'sommets principaux' labels the marked points on the large circle (vertices of the cyclically reduced core).
The phrase after (Γ_i)_{i∈I} is uncertain; it may read 'famille d'arbres ponctués' rather than 'arbres plans'.
